meta.title: Who really said "Teach a Parrot to Say 'Supply and Demand' and You Have an Economist"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Carlyle. The joke is documented from 1907 in Irving Fisher’s The Rate of Interest, told anonymously. Carlyle’s name arrives in 1931.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Teach a Parrot to Say 'Supply and Demand' and You Have an Economist'?
meta.ogDescription: Carlyle died in 1881; the parrot joke is first documented in 1907 as an anonymous quip, and pinned on him only in 1931 — hedged as “probably”.

answer.label: Not Thomas Carlyle — an anonymous economists’ joke
answer.authorDates: In print by 1907 · attributed to Carlyle from 1931
answer.sourceLine: Thomas Carlyle died in 1881, and no version of this joke has been found in anything he wrote. The earliest documented instance, located by Quote Investigator ↗ and read by us in the scanned first edition ↗, is in Irving Fisher’s The Rate of Interest (1907), page 6, where Fisher introduces it as something “once wittily remarked” and names nobody. Carlyle’s name was attached in 1931 by an author who wrote only that it was “probably” his.

source.excerpt: It was once wittily remarked of the early writers on economic problems, “Catch a parrot and teach him to say ‘supply and demand,’ and you have an excellent economist.” Prices, wages, rent, interest, and profits were thought to be fully “explained” by this glib phrase.
trail: The earliest documented instance Quote Investigator ↗ locates is in Irving Fisher’s The Rate of Interest (1907), page 6. We read the page in the scanned first edition ↗ and confirmed Fisher gives no originator.
Fisher expanded the joke in his 1910 textbook Introduction to Economic Science, prefacing it “a long time ago” — an assertion he did not support with a citation, per Quote Investigator ↗.

The first appearance of Carlyle’s name is in Frank Albert Fetter’s The Masquerade of Monopoly (1931), in a chapter titled “Teach a Parrot”: “It was probably Thomas Carlyle’s none too gentle pen that first wrote…” The hedge is Fetter’s own, per Quote Investigator ↗.
Wikiquote’s Thomas Carlyle page ↗ documents no version of the parrot joke anywhere — though it does carry his genuine and quite different remarks on supply and demand in Past and Present.
source.excerptNote: Irving Fisher, The Rate of Interest (New York: Macmillan, 1907), page 6, read in the scanned edition ↗. Fisher attributes the remark to nobody — “it was once wittily remarked” — which is the strongest single piece of evidence that no author was known even then.

source.rightsNote: The joke has no identifiable author, so no rights status can be asserted for it. Irving Fisher’s The Rate of Interest (1907), which carries the earliest documented wording, was published well before 1931 and is in the public domain in the United States; the 1931 Fetter phrasing that first names Carlyle is not.

author.name: Anonymous
author.heading: About the author — and why there isn’t one
author.metaLine: Unidentified · earliest documented instance in Irving Fisher, The Rate of Interest, 1907
author.bio: Nobody knows who built this joke. It arrives fully formed in Irving Fisher’s 1907 treatise on interest, introduced as something “once wittily remarked” by an unnamed critic of the early economists. Quote Investigator’s reading is that it condensed out of a much older habit — running back to at least 1850 — of calling “supply and demand” a parrot word.

copyAttribution: An anonymous economists' joke, in print by 1907 — attributed to Thomas Carlyle only in 1931, fifty years after his death.

misattribution.heading: Why Carlyle gets the credit — and why it does not hold
misattribution.intro: Carlyle coined “the dismal science” for economics and spent much of his career attacking exactly the kind of thinking the joke mocks, which makes him an irresistible candidate. The chronology rules him out.

items.why: No version of the joke has been found in Carlyle’s published work, and the first person to connect him to it, Frank Fetter in 1931, said only that it was “probably” his. That is fifty years after Carlyle’s death in 1881, and Quote Investigator ↗ reports no substantive support for the ascription.

items.who: An anonymous quip, in print by 1907
items.why: Irving Fisher printed it in The Rate of Interest in 1907 as something “once wittily remarked”, with no name attached. Quote Investigator ↗ suggests it grew out of a much older habit, running back to at least 1850, of dismissing “supply and demand” as mere “parrot words”.

A 1992 New York Times review of a Schumpeter biography listed “Catch a parrot, teach him to say ‘Supply and Demand’ and you have an economist” among his savage aphorisms, without crediting him with coinage, per Quote Investigator ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The joke was already circulating anonymously in 1907; Carlyle’s name was attached in 1931 with the word “probably”, and nothing has been found to support it since, per Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The joke is a complaint about explanation. Fisher introduces it in the middle of an argument that “supply and demand” had become a phrase economists reached for to cover problems they could not actually solve — his own words are that it “has been too often forced into service to cover up difficult problems”.
That is why the parrot is the right image: the bird produces the correct answer to every question, and understands none of them. The gag survives because the complaint keeps being true.
detailsBody: The parrot was insulting economists long before the joke existed. Quote Investigator ↗ records “parrot words” used of supply and demand in 1850, “parrot-like” by a Knights of Labor official in 1886, “parrot-cries” in 1893, and a reviewer in 1897 comparing an author to “a trained parrot”. The joke looks like the point at which a stock metaphor was turned into a scene.

The wording kept moving even after 1907. A 1928 version made the parrot a business man rather than an economist; Fetter’s 1931 chapter turned it back on the United States Steel Corporation; and by 1950 a textbook was crediting it simply to “a noted economist”.
context.pull: The parrot gives the right answer to every question, and understands none of them.
